parole.significato: a suffix appended to words to create an agent noun, much like English -er/-or
parole.testo: Likely from Latin -ārius.

parole.significato: Forms nouns from verbs, chiefly action nouns and result nouns. Now unproductive.
parole.testo: Found suffixed exclusively to verbs loaned from Latin verbs in the first conjugation, -ō, -āre, hence likely itself borrowed from Latin -āta n pl (“-ed things”). Compare gjykatë (“court”), akin to Romanian judecată (“judgement; court”), and note also Italian -ata often used found in the same deverba

parole.significato: forms female equivalents to male nouns. -ess
parole.testo: From Late Latin -issa. Compare Romanian -easă, Italian -essa.
From Latin -ōnea, -ōnia, whence Romanian -oaie and Aromanian -oanji -oanje -onje.
Learned borrowing from Latin -tās, -tātis. Doublet of -tet.
Derived from Vulgar Latin -torius, -torium.
From Latin abacus or Italian abaco.
Learned borrowing from Latin abdicō (“abdicate”).
From Late Latin abyssus.

It seems to be a complicated compound *a-bonus-ina, a derivation of Latin bonus with a similar development as Romanian pa bune "for real", creating the prefix a- and with an adverbial suffix -ina (Standard -irë), often used in Archaic Gheg.
Learned borrowing from Latin abrogō (“abrogate”).
Learned borrowing from Latin absolūtus.
Learned borrowing from Latin absorbeō.
Learned borrowing from Latin abstentus.
Learned borrowing from Latin abstineō (“abstain”).
Learned borrowing from Latin abstractus.
Learned borrowing from Latin absurditās.
Learned borrowing from Latin abūsus.
Learned borrowing from Latin aciditātem, accusative singular of aciditās (“sourness, acidity”), from acidus (“sour, acid”), or through French acidité. See acid.
Borrowed from Latin adamās, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “diamond”).

Borrowed from Latin adōrāre (“revere, admire, adore”) or Italian adorare (“adore”). According to Orel, it is a learned borrowing from Latin. Attested in Buzuku's Missal as adoronj (influenced by the Italian cognate), while other old authors use the popular term adhëronj.
Learned borrowing from Latin administrātiō.
Mediopassive form of active admiroj (“to admire”). Learned borrowing from Latin admīror.
Active form of mediopassive admirohem (“to be admired”). Learned borrowing from Latin admiror.
Ultimately borrowed from a derivative of Latin ad directus, from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre, from Classical Latin dīrēctus (“straight”). Compare French adresse.

Borrowed from Latin āēr (“air”), ultimately derived from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). Topalli posits Italian aria (“air”) as another possible source, considering that the Latin term is already (potentially) borrowed into Albanian as erë (“wind, air, smell”); alternatively, it is a doublet.
Modern learned borrowing from Latin acācia, from Ancient Greek ἀκακία (akakía).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin amia (“sea fish”), derived from Ancient Greek ἀμία (amía).
Probably borrowed from Latin amiantus, ultimately from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μῐ́ᾰντος (ămĭ́ăntos).
From amë (“source; mother; stub”) + -zë. Sense 1 is likely a calque of Latin mātrīcula (“register”).

Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin aurum (“gold”). Considering the rendering of Latin au- as Albanian ā-, it is a relatively archaic borrowing. Although Arbëresh dialects preserve the original Latin neuter, in standard Albanian it is masculine.

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin argentum (“silver”). The modern form is possibly borrowed from Italian argento (“silver”), whereas the older form rgjand was directly loaned from Latin. Considering the attested argjand, a prothetic a- (compare Buzuku's ergjand) or contamination from the Italia
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin arca (“chest, box, coffin”).
From Medieval Latin armāta; possibly through the intermediate of Italian armata.
From an earlier anëmik, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin inimīcus (“enemy”).
Borrowed from Late Latin arma (“weapon”). A later loan from Italian arma (“weapon”) is also plausible.

parole.significato: to patch, mend, doctor, cobble, restore
parole.testo: Perhaps from arnë (“patch”) + -oj, ultimately a derivative of harr (“to weed”). But more likely borrowed from Latin renovāre (“to renew, restore, revive”), which is supported by the form of the aorist, as well as the more conservative spelling arënoj, which would make arnë a back-formation.
According to Çabej, a derivative of harr (“to weed”). Alternatively a back formation of arnoj (“to patch”), borrowed from Latin renovāre (“to renew, restore, revive”).

parole.significato: education (process or art of imparting knowledge, skill and judgment)
parole.testo: Gerund of arsej (“to teach, give knowledge”), from arsye (“reason”), itself a borrowing from the accusative Latin ratiōnem of Latin ratiō.
Learned borrowing from Latin ars, artem.
Learned borrowing from Latin articulus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin artista or French artiste, ultimately from Latin ars.
Borrowed from Latin asbestos, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄσβεστος (ásbestos).
From Latin asper (“rough, uneven”).
From Latin atrophia.
Learned borrowing from Latin auctor.

parole.significato: authority (the power to enforce rules or give orders)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin auctōritās.

parole.significato: to advance (to move forwards, to approach)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante. Perhaps borrowed through Venetan or another Romance language.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin aulamentum, a derivative of Latin aulaeum (“canopy, covering, courtain”) with the suffix -mentum that denotes an instrument, medium, or result.
Borrowed from French avocat, from Latin advocātus.
From Latin barathrum (“chasm, pit, hell”), derived from Ancient Greek βάραθρον (bárathron, “gulf, cleft, pit”).
By surface analysis, banjë (“bath”) + -tar. Possibly borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin balneātor (“bath attendant”).
From Vulgar Latin baneum, variant of Latin balneum. Compare Romanian baie f, Proto-Slavic *baňa f. Semantic loan from Italian bagno in many senses.
Calque of Latin cōnsonāns (or of German Mitlaut?) via bashkë- + tingëllor.
From bekoj + -im, bekoj a borrowing from Latin benedīcō.

Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin benedicō (“to bless, praise”). A more phonologically conserved variant is bënkoj, whereas the standard form was possibly affected by be (“oath”) considering the lack of reduction of the unstressed vowel.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin battālia, variant of Latin battuālia, from Latin battuō. Compare Romanian bătaie, Aromanian bãtalje.
Seemingly from Latin occurring twice; in pairs. The first element bi- ("two(fold)") also occurs in binjak.

parole.significato: A biographer (the writer of a biography).
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin biographus or Ancient Greek βιογράφος (biográphos).

parole.significato: encore (brief extra performance after the main performance is complete)
parole.testo: From Latin bis (“twice; again!”).

Uncertain, but cognate to Romanian păstaie (“pod”), Aromanian pãstalji (“pod”): * Possibly borrowed from Vulgar Latin *pī̆stālia (whence also the (A)Romanian words), from Late Latin pī̆stāre (“to pound”), frequentative of Latin pīnsāre (“to stamp, pound, crush”), but this is semantically questionabl
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin bīstia (compare Italian biscia, French biche), from Latin bēstia.
From Medieval Latin bisōn.
From Latin oblāta (“shown, offered”) with various meanings, though "seal" remains an unclear development.
Borrowed from Latin brāca or brācae, likely ultimately from Proto-Germanic *brōks (> English breeches). Compare also dialectal Romanian brace, and cf. the verb îmbrăca.

A derivation of bri (“horn”), contaminated with brinjë (“rib”, literally “horn-shaped or semicircular halo over one's head”). Alternatively, it might be an irregular derivation of Latin aurora, with a strong change in pronunciation similar to Ancient Greek αὔρα (aúra). The evolution could have been
Probably borrowed from a Vulgar Latin *brosca, or *broscus, broxae (“frog”) (compare Romanian broască, Old French bruesche, Milanese Lombard brosco), from Ionic Ancient Greek βρόθακος (bróthakos).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin brūma. Compare Romanian brumă.
Borrowed from Late Latin būfus (“owl”), probably of onomatopoeic origin; see also Ancient Greek βοῦφος (boûphos). Compare archaic Romanian buf, Spanish búho.
Learned borrowing from Latin centuria.
From Late Latin cyclus.
Ultimately from Latin deus.
Learned borrowing from Latin debilis (“weak, frail, feeble”).
Learned borrowing from Latin delphinus.
From Latin dignus.

Historically attested as derpëtonj, debërtonj, derpërtonj, which go back to a common *ndërpërtonj from the adverb ndërpër (“through”) (modern nëpër). Orel suggests a borrowing from an unattested Vulgar Latin *depenetrō (compare Latin penetrō).
Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin root *dēbitura, from Latin dēbitus. Also possibly through the intermediate of an Eastern Romance language; compare Romanian datorie.

PIE word  *wek(ʷ)speros Probably via some Balkan Vulgar Latin dialect, ultimately borrowed from Latin vesper or Ancient Greek ἕσπερος (hésperos), with internal /v/ > /ð/ backing. Compare dhelpër for the same phenomenon.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin discus, from Ancient Greek δίσκος (dískos). Compare German Tisch (“table”) and English dish. Doublet of dishtë.
Calque of Latin December, from dhjetë (“ten”) + -or.
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin doga, ultimately from Ancient Greek. Compare also Italian doga, Romanian doagă, Dalmatian duag.
Borrowed from Latin dōnātiō. Equivalent to dhuroj + -atë.
Possibly borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin dōnō. Otherwise related to Proto-Albanian *dhu̯onti (dhunti), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- (“to give”).
Learned borrowing from Latin diabētēs (“siphon”).
Borrowed from New Latin diathesis, from Ancient Greek διάθεσις (diáthesis, “state, condition”), from διατίθημι (diatíthēmi, “to arrange”).
Borrwom from Latin dignitātem. Displaced native Albanian erz.
Probably from an earlier dishkë given the Albanian -k-, Latin -c- correspondance, from Vulgar Latin, from Latin discus (“disc”). Doublet of dhisk.
From Vulgar Latin disculus (“small disk”). Variants dyshkull, dushkull and ndryshkull result from folk etymologies relating to dushk (“oak”) or ndryshk (“rust”).
From earlier djemënë, from Latin daemōn. Exclusive to the Gheg Catholic community.

From Sicilian Medieval Latin doana, dovana (attested from the end of the 12th century), from Andalusian Arabic *duwān, an alteration of the Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān, “administrative office”), borrowed from Classical Persian دیوان (dēwān, dīwān, “customs, divan”).
Borrowed from Latin doctor.
Calque of Latin manualē; dorë (“hand”) + -cak.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin dīrēctus.
From Late Latin drictus, from Latin dīrēctus, through Dalmatian *draita, variant of drat.
Singularized plural of *drak, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin dracō. Compare Romanian drac.
From Latin Drivastum, although it has been noted that the accentual pattern found in Drísht < Drívastum presupposes an Adriatic "Illyrian" intermediary.
Possibly borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin ductus (“conveyance of water, channel”) per Meyer. More likely from Latin ducem, which has developed similar meanings in other Romance languages.
Borrowed from Latin dūrāre, with an irregular reflex of Latin -ū-.
Under influence of dushk (“oak”) altered from dishull, from Vulgar Latin disculus (“small disk”). Along with variants dyshkull and ndryshkull influenced by dushk (“oak”) or ndryshk (“rust”).

First attested as ëndiglonj in Buzuku, borrowed from Vulgar Latin intellegō (“to understand, perceive”), with metathesis of the -l- and -g- and many other phonological distortions in dialects, with the predominant form ultimately phonologically contaminated with gjoj (“to hear”).

Disputed: * From an earlier *dërkoj, from darkë. Related to ndikoj (“to pour in, to influence”) and dikoj (“to flow, to pour”). Same sense development as in derdh, with secondary meanings being "to strike down", "to cause to fall". * Borrowed from Latin indīcere (“to impose, to inflict”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin deliberāre.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin damnum.

Explained as a borrowing from a Vulgar Latin verb derived from Latin dīrigō (“to lay straight, direct, distribute”) through an earlier Proto-Albanian *dər(ə)goɲ;. Orel suggests a borrowing from Latin dēlēgō (“to send”) with an irregular change of the liquid consonant.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin dēsīderō. Compare Italian desiderare, desirare, archaic Romanian deșidera.
From dëshiroj or possibly Latin dēsīderium.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin testimōniāre, from Latin testimōnium.
Calque of Latin diēs Sōlis, based on Albanian diell.
Calque of Latin diēs Lūnae, based on Albanian hënë.
From Vulgar Latin, from Latin (diēs) Mercuriī. Compare Romanian miercuri, Aromanian Njercuri.

Probably a calque of Latin diēs Veneris. From earlier variants e prende or e prente, from the name of Prenda, a pagan goddess protector of women, from Proto-Indo-European *prāy-, *prēy- (“to like, love”). Cognate with Proto-Germanic *Frijjō (cf. Old Norse Freyja (“lady, mistress”), English Friday),

Unknown. The standard opinion assumes a borrowing through Vulgar Latin from Latin dies Saturni. However, the assumption that Latin -rn- would lead to Albanian -n- is untenable, as the expected outcome would be -rr-; *e shturrë (see burrë (“man”), varrë (“wound”), ferr (“hell”), furrë (“oven”)).
Learned borrowing from Latin elephantem. Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin amita (“paternal aunt”). Though, the change from a- > e- is troublesome.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin ēsca.

From dialectal (Cham) fal, from Vulgar Latin *fallia, deverbal of Latin fallere; compare French faille (“fault”), Italian faglia (“fault”), Aromanian fai f (“fault, sin”). Less likely from Gothic 𐍆𐌰𐌹𐌰𐌽 (faian, “to blame”).
Borrowed from Latin falsus (“counterfeit, false; falsehood”), perfect passive participle of fallō (“deceive”).
Learned borrowing from Latin familia; cf. Italian famiglia. Doublet of fëmijë, an older borrowing from Vulgar Latin.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin famulus.
Borrowed from Latin phantasma, from Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma, “image, phantom”), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to make visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to cause to appear, bring to light”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin facia (“face”).
Borrowed from Latin Pharus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Classical Latin fabrica, with regular loss of word-internal /b/ before /r/. Compare the later borrowing fabrikë (“factory”), likely from Italian.

Borrowed via Vulgar Latin from Latin fascia (“band, bandage”). Also attested as fashqe (“diaper”) (which, per Orel, is a singularized plural from *fashqë). Compare Romanian fașă, with the same pronunciation.
Borrowed from Latin fātum. Jolk claims a derivation from Gothic fadi-.

parole.significato: a female (individual belonging to the sex that can typically give birth)
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin femina (“woman”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin īnfernus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin festum. Cognate to French fête, Italian festa, English fest and the like.
Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin root *fīliānus, from Latin fīlius. Compare Romanian fin.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin fīcus.
Borrowed from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
From Late Latin fistulare (fiscla (“whistle”), Italian fischiare (“whistle”)).
Ultimately from Latin victoria, via a Balkan Romance language.
A formation similar to fletë and flugë. A loanword from Latin through Vulgar Latin may be plausible too, cf. facula; compare Romanian flacără, Italian fiaccola.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin floccus. Compare Romanian floc.
Uncertain. Possibly a Latin borrowing, from Latin formella (“small form”).
Derived from Latin fōrmō. Equivalent to formë + -oj.
First attested in 1555 by Buzuku. Borrowed from Latin forma (“form”). Alternative opinions opt for an Italian borrowing, though with less support.
Borrowed from Latin fortis.
It reflects an unattested *fosh that may result (irregularly as far as the anlaut is concerned) from *ftosh, the latter being a borrowing from Latin fētōsus, to fētus (“offspring”).
Unknown. Perhaps from Latin vīcīnus, related to or derived from fqinj, with a meaning of "hospitality" or "friendliness". Standard Albanian is ngushëlloj.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin vīcīnus.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin fraxinus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin frēnum. Compare Romanian frâu.
From Vulgar Latin *friscum.
Ultimately from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos).
Unknown. Maybe from Vulgar Latin *ferrusca (“small iron”), from Latin ferrum.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin fructus. Doublet of frutë, which was a later borrowing.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin vessīca, variant of vēsīca. Compare Romanian bășică.
Borrowed from Latin ventilō.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin invitō.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cotōneus, cotōneum. The change k → f before /t/ is regular.
Related to fugë (“fire”). Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *focāria. Compare Italian focolare.
Borrowed from Latin fundus.
Borrowed from Latin furca.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin furnus.
Ultimately from Latin fortūna. Compare Romanian furtună, Greek φουρτούνα (fourtoúna), Turkish fırtına.

Orel claims it is borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin fossa (“ditch, moat”). However, Çabej identifies it as an inherited word from Proto-Albanian *pl̥thu̯iām. Matasović claims it has no known etymology. Possibly from Arabic فُسْحَة (fusḥa, “wide, spatious place”).

parole.significato: kind of fishing spear consisting of a long shaft with many hooked extremities
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin fuscina.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin fūsus.
From fyt (“throat”). Influenced by and alternatively borrowed from Latin factūra (“making, manufacture”) (compare Romanian Romanian făptură (“creature, form”), Italian Italian fattura (“make”)).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin familia (“family”). Compare also Romanian femeie, Aromanian fumealji, fumelj. Doublet of familje.
Possibly Italian fango from borrowed from Vulgar Latin *fangus (“mud”). Jokl claims a borrowing from Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌲𐌲𐍃 (waggs, “paradise, *meadow”), from Proto-Germanic *wangaz (“field, meadow”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin fenestra. Doublet of finestër.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin frīgō (“to roast, fry”). Compare Romanian frige, French frire, English fry.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *frīgulō, from Latin frīgeō. Compare French friller.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin fricō. Compare Romanian freca.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin form *carabriōnem, from Latin crābrōnem.
Calque of Latin paenīnsula; from gati (“nearly”) + ishull (“island”) with seemingly irregular voiced -d-.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin galgulus, from galbulus. Compare Romanian grangur, Spanish gálgulo.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin gaudium.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin gallus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin galbinus. Compare Romanian galben.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin genius.
From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

parole.significato: people (a group of persons forming or belonging to a particular nation etc.)
parole.testo: From Latin gens (“id”).
From Latin gentem. Cognate to Italian gente, Spanish gente, and others.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *genía (“generation, clan”), compare Sicilian jinìa, Italian genia.

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin cicāla, from Latin cicāda (“cicada”), with metathesis of voicedness from the more conservative form qingallë. The unetymological -n- may have been inserted by contamination with qengj, qingj (“lamb”).
Unknown. Possibly from Latin garrio.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin iūdicātus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin jūdicō ("judge, pass judgment, proclaim").
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin jūnctūra.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium. Compare Romanian județ.

parole.significato: to collect bit by bit, gather
parole.testo: From Latin collīmitāre (“to draw boundaries, *to unite”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin glandula. Compare also Romanian ghindură, Aromanian gljindurã.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin Gothī.
From Vulgar Latin *grāma (see Spanish grama) from earlier Latin grāmĭna, plural of grāmen.
From Latin graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós). Ultimately forms a doublet of gërk.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin grex, gregem.

Unknown; possibly: * borrowed from Vulgar Latin *cremorātum, from Latin cremor (“porridge, stew; thick liquid”), * from earlier *glëmëratë with liquid assimilation, borrowed from Latin glomerātum, participle of glomerāre (“make into a ball, pile in a heap”).
From Latin collūctārī, present infinitive of collūctor (“to struggle, contend”). A doublet of gulçoj.
From Vulgar Latin *colluctiāre, from collūctārī, present infinitive of collūctor (“to struggle, contend”). A doublet of gultoj.
From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Compare Romanian gust, popular alternative name for the month of August.
Unknown. Maybe from Latin jūstus.
Ultimately from Latin gutta.
Borrowed from Latin cottizare, from Ancient Greek κοττίζω (kottízō).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin calcāria (“lime quarry”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin ingannō, from Latin ganniō. Compare Romanian îngâna.
With epenthetic -r- from variant gësherë, from Late Latin cīsōria, plural of cīsōrium (“shear, scissor”). Compare Italian cesoie (“shears”), French cisoires (“bench shears”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin castanea, from Ancient Greek καστάνεια (kastáneia). Compare Aromanian cãstãnji.
From Latin gaudium.
From dialectal harmëshor, from Old Albanian harmëshuar, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *armissārius (compare Romanian armăsar), from Latin admissārius.
Learned borrowing from Latin hepar (“liver”).

Borrowed from Latin hōra (“hour, time, season”), through Vulgar Latin with unexplained preservation of h or more likely the coincidental reappearance by other means. Cognate with Romanian oară. Doublet of orë (“hour, clock, watch”), a recent borrowing.
From Vulgar Latin *hinniculare (compare Neapolitan annechiare, Sardinian innicrare), diminutive of Latin hinnīre.
Learned borrowing from Latin historia.
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin iocus. Compare English joke.
From Latin idolum, from Ancient Greek εἴδωλον (eídōlon, “image, idol”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin īlia, plural of īle. Compare archaic Romanian ie.
Singularized plural of *ilqë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin īlicem.
Borrowed from Latin altārium.
Learned borrowing from Latin imāginor.
Learned borrowing from Latin interpretor.
Either from a lost transitive Romance verb *iranare, from Latin ira. Otherwise a derivative of irë (“wrath, heroism”) or related to irnohem.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *isula, from Latin insula.
Ultimately from Latin Iānuārius (“January”).
From Latin ēcho, ultimately from Ancient Greek ἠχώ (ēkhṓ). Used as a basis for jehoj (“to echo”) and jehonë (“echo”).
From jeh, from Latin ēchō.
By surface analysis, jeh + -onë, but compare Latin ēchōnis, genitive singular of Latin ēchō.
Learned borrowing from Latin iustificō.
From an older kallënduor, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin calendārium. Compare archaic/popular Romanian cărindar (“id.”). Doublet of kalendar.
From Late Latin or Vulgar Latin caballāricius, from Latin caballus (“horse”), whence Albanian kalë. Compare Aromanian cãlãrets, Romanian călăreț.
From earlier *kaltënë, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *calthinus (“yellow, yellowish”), from Latin caltha (“marigold”). Ultimately from Ancient Greek κάλαθος (kálathos).

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Late Latin caballus (“horse”). Topalli suggests Gheg plural kual borrowed from Italian descendant cavallo, with phonetic development *këval > *kval > kual, whereas Tosk and standard kuaj was influenced by buaj, plural of buall (“bull”). Compare Romanian cal, Aromania
Learned borrowing from Latin candidatus.

parole.significato: jar, cruse, vessel, oil jar (most common usage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin cantharus (“large drinking vessel, tankard, pot”). According to Çabej directly from Ancient Greek κάνθαρος (kántharos, “drinking cup”).

parole.significato: song: part of an epic poetry piece
parole.testo: Borrowed from Vulgar Latin canticellum (compare Romanian cântecel). According to Çabej an Albanian derivative of këngë with suffix -el.
Possibly borrowed from Latin cāpus, archaic form of cāpō (“rooster”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin capreolus ("roe deer, roe buck").
Borrowed from Latin carota.
Borrowed from Latin carrūca or Italian carrozza (“carriage”) with semantic conflation with Italian carrozzina (“pram; wheelchair”).
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin charta. Compare Romanian carte.

parole.significato: hood of a cloak or raincoat
parole.testo: Plurale tantum; from Latin casula (“hooded cloak”). Doublet of kësulë.
From Latin carrus, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *karros (“wagon”).
From earlier klishë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).
From Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára).

Learned borrowing from Latin classis (“a class or division of the people, assembly of people, the whole body of citizens called to arms, the army, the fleet, later a class or division in general”), from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to call, shout”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *codrum whence Romanian codru (“forest; morsel”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Latin coxa (“hip”). Compare Romanian coapsă.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *coctōrium (“oven”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin coquus (“cook”).

Originally only “spherical object”, thought to be borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin coccum (“scarlet berry, gall”). However, due to strong semantical parallels and on geographic grounds, it is perhaps more likely to be derived directly from Ancient Greek κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed, berry”).
Borrowed from Latin coma (“hair”).
Learned borrowing from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”).
Ultimately from Latin commūnālis (“communal”), from commūnis (“common, shared”) + -ālis (“-al”), with influence from komunë in reference to local government.

parole.significato: municipality, a first-level administrative division of Kosovo
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin commūne.
Learned borrowing from Latin cōnsistō through English consist.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin corvus. Compare Romanian corb, Italian corvo.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin corbis (which might have given dialectal korbe) + suffix -ull.
From Latin chorda (“gut, catgut”).
From Latin cichorēum ~ cichorium.
Possibly from Latin quartus.
From Latin corpus.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *quaresima, from Latin quadrāgēsima (“Lent, forty-day fast”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin crista. Compare Romanian creastă.

parole.significato: to come up with, to conceive, to devise
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin creō.
From earlier krështerë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin Chrīstiānus.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin croculum, diminutive of Latin crocus.

parole.significato: bride's father or bridegroom's father; male family member of either
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin consocer, consocerum. Compare Romanian cuscru.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin crux, crucem, with an irregular substitution of the short Latin -u-.
From older kuor(r). According to Çabej and Demiraj from a derivative of korr According to Orel from Latin chorus (“dance in a ring, harmony, harmonious motion”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin incus, incudem (“anvil”).
Enlargement of kudh, from Latin incus, incudem (“anvil”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin confīnis.

Borrowed from Latin cōgitō, through the intermediary stages of Proto-Albanian *kugitānja > *kugj(ë)tonj > *kuqtonj > kujtoj. The dialectal variant kultoj is due to a hypercorrection of the original form kujtoj. Compare Romanian cugeta, Spanish cuidar.
From Latin cucullus, via Greek κουκούλι. Doublet of kukull.
Borrowed from Late Latin cucurum or Byzantine Greek κούκουρον (koúkouron). See Proto-Mongolic *kökexür for more.

Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin *cucūta, from Latin cicūta. Also possibly from a local Eastern Romance language intermediate; compare Romanian cucută, Aromanian cucutã, with close similarity of pronunciation.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin collāre, from Latin collāris.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cōlō (“to filter, strain”).
Borrowed from Latin colostrum.
Derivative of *kullumbë borrowed from Latin columba (“dove, pigeon”). The fruit is called after the bird because of its bluish colour, cf. Romanian porumbă (“sloe”) after palumbes (“dove”).
A metathesis of *kullumesë (cf. gjysmë) borrowed from Vulgar Latin columnātia (cf. Latin columnātiō).
From Latin culmen.
From Late Latin culcitra (“mattress, pillow”), itself a form of Latin culcita.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin commonitus.
Old borrowing from Latin compater (“godfather”), itself from com- + pater (“father”).
Borrowed from Latin cognātus. Compare Romanian cumnat, Aromanian cumnat, Dalmatian comnut.
From Latin cūnctārī (“to delay, hesitate”).
Borrowed from Latin contrā.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin commūnicō (“to impart, to share”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cuneus. Compare Romanian cui.
Borrowed from Latin computō (“to compute, reckon”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin cuppa, from Latin cūpa.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin cocceus, from Latin coccum.
From Old Albanian kunorë (preserved in Gheg), from Latin corōna (“garland, crown”). The sense marriage derives from Byzantine tradition.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin constāre.

Apparently a contraction of kush â trim (who is brave?), the traditional call when some danger presented itself. Orel derives it from the gerund of an unattested *kushtroj: *kushtroj + -im, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *conscrīptāre, a secondary formation based on conscrībere (“to enroll, enlist”).
Borrowed from Latin cōnsobrīnus (“first cousin, relation”).
From archaic kut, from Latin cubitus.
From Late Latin contentāre.
From kulshedër, from Late Latin celsydri, blend of Ancient Greek χέλυδρος (khéludros, “poisonous”) + χέρσυδρος (khérsudros, “amphibious snake”).

Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin campāna (“stilyard; bell”), from Latin Campāna, feminine of Campānus (“of Campania”), from Campānia (“a region of Italy in which bronze was produced”), from campus (“open or flat space; plain”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin camisia (“shirt”).
Various existing etymologies: * From Medieval Latin cannata. * From Turkish kanata. * An internal formation from kanë (“type of pitcher”).
From a noun *këndell(i), borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin candela (“light, fire”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin, from Latin cantāre.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin cannētum (“reed field”). Tosk's rhotacism (-n- > -r-), impacting an intervocalic -n-, was prevented by Latin's double -nn-.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin cantica (“song”). Compare Romanian cântec.

parole.significato: to look for, to seek, to search for
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin circō, from Latin circus, circa.
From an earlier *kanëp (compare also Romanian cânepă), borrowed from Vulgar Latin canapa, from Latin cannabis, derived from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis). See there for more. Gheg kanp.
Back-formation of *këshij (interpreted as a plural form), borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin consilium.

Borrowed from Latin castellum (“castle”). The modern form, ending in -ll, is influenced in part by Italian castello. Old Albanian kështjel (Buzuku) and këshqel show no Italian influence. An origin from Italian instead is unfavorable due to the -a- > -ë-, -e- > -je-, and -s- > -sh- changes, which sho
Borrowed from Latin clausura.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin laxa (“loose”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin lapis.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin laurus.

parole.significato: far, far away, afar, away. in space or time
parole.testo: Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin largus (“abundant, big”, adjective). Compare Aromanian largu (“far”, adverb).
Ultimately from Latin Latīnus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin laus, laudem.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin, from Latin laus, laudem.

Uncertain. The original form was likely lend m and lende arose as a back-formation from its plural. The variant with vl- is almost certainly secondary. # Akin to other Indo-European terms for “lentil”, such as Latin lēns, lentis, Lithuanian lę̃šis, German Linse, though the ultimate origin is unclear
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin leporem. Aromanian ljepuri and Romanian iepure.
From Albanian lepur borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin leporem, with the suffix of Albanian -ush.
Borrowed from Latin litterārius (“literary”). By surface analysis, letër (“paper, letter”) + -ar or letra pl (“letters, literature”) + -ar.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin līnum.
Borrowed through Late Vulgar Latin (or Old Italian) from Latin liber.
From Latin līneus or līnea.

From Latin Ulpiāna, from Ulpius, the nomen gentilicium of Trajan + -ānus. Selami Pulaha states that the shift from Ulpiana to Lipjan is in accordance with early Albanian phonetic rules, and must therefore have been inhabited by Albanians to reach its current form. It has also been connected with the
Alteration of dialectal lucë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin lutea.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin leō, leōnem.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin luctārī. By surface analysis, luftë + -oj.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Late Latin lucta, from Latin luctor; cognate with Romanian luptă, Aromanian ljuftã.

parole.significato: revenant: a spiteful person who rises from the grave after death and terrorizes people, zombie, vampire
parole.testo: According to Orel, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *lupus peccatus (“false wolf”), though with difficult semantics.
From Latin lucrum (“gain, profit, wealth”). Compare also Romanian and Aromanian lucru (“thing”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin from Latin lunter, luntrem; compare Romanian luntre, Italian londra.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin lutra (“otter”). Compare Italian lontra (“otter”).

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *lupus cervulus, from lupus cervārius (“lynx”) (compare French loup-cervier, Italian lupo cerviero, Romansh luf tscherver), from Latin lupus + cervārius < cervus. Doublet of rrëqebull (“lynx”).
From Latin lucerna (“(oil) lamp”).
Borrowed from Latin līmāre.
From lëngatë + -oj. Orel claims a borrowing through Vulgar Latin from Latin languēre.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin labōrō. Compare meaning in Spanish labrar, French labourer, Occitan laurar.

Borrowed from Latin laxō, laxāre (“to let”), via its byform *lassō, *lassāre, evidenced by Romanian lăsa, Aromanian alas, dialectal Italian lassare. Many scholars also consider the possibility of a borrowing from Italian lasciare, although it is less likely due to the term's early attestation date a
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin Latīnus. Doublet of latín.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin laudō. Compare Romanian lăuda, Aromanian alavdu.
From Latin Maius. Compare Aromanian maiu, Romanian mai, Greek Μάιος (Máios).
From Latin malleus. Compare Romanian mai, Italian maglio.
From Latin malleator (“hammerer”). By surface analysis, máj (“hammer”) + -tór.
Probably a learned borrowing from Latin māchina, ultimately from Doric Greek μᾱχᾰνᾱ́ (mākhănā́). Doublet of mokër.
Borrowed from Latin malum.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin maledīcō.
Borrowed from Latin mancus (“maimed, infirm”); doublet of mënk ‘one-armed’.
Plurale tantum; plural of variant marë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin marum (“cat thyme, kind of sage”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin Mārtius (“March”).

parole.significato: to marry off, cause to get married, marry
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin marītō. Compare meaning in Romanian mărita.
Borrowed from Latin (diēs) Mārtis.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin masculus. The Proto-Albanian singular was *maśkulʉh, plural *maśkuli.
Probably borrowed from a Vulgar Latin root *masteru-, from Latin magister (“master”).
Ultimately from Latin invidia.
From Vulgar Latin *imperātus (compare Romanian împărat, Aromanian ampirat), from Latin imperātor.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin milium.

parole.significato: man (who has just become a father)
parole.testo: Ffrom Latin maricosus.
Ultimately from Latin Mercurius.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin missa, from Latin missus.
Learned borrowing from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mīlia, plural of mīlle, evolving internally in Albanian through /ˈmiʎə/, still retained in some Albanian archaic varieties. Compare Romanian mie.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin amīcus (“friend”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin minūta.

parole.significato: fourth wife; that would be wed to a Christian without a lawful union
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus or directly from Italian amorosa.
From Latin mors, mortem.
Borrowed through through Vulgar Latin from Latin mors, mortem. Compare Romanian moarte, Italian morte.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *mōstra, from Latin mōnstrum.
From Old Albanian mërekull, borrowed from Latin mīrāculum.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin molāris.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin molīnum, from Latin molō.

parole.significato: to be absent, to be missed
parole.testo: Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus (“maimed, powerless”). Cf. also Italian mancare (“to lack”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Late Latin monachus.
From murg + -eshë, and Tosk variant of Gheg mûng, from Late Latin monāchus, from Ancient Greek μοναχός (monakhós).
Borrowed from Latin murmurāre.

parole.significato: strong north wind, cold wind, gale
parole.testo: According to Orel, the form murrë ~ murrâ is borrowed with an assimilation of the initial b- from Latin boreanus (“Borean”), an adjectival formation of Latin boreās (“north wind”). However, this is highly improbable.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mortālia, from mortālis.

Variant of mushkull, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin musculus (“muscle”). Compare Romanian mușchi, Aromanian mushclju, cf. also Catalan muscle (“shoulder”). Doublet of muskul, a later learned borrowing.
Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin root *musconea, from Latin musca, or through a local Eastern Romance language; compare Aromanian mushconj.

parole.significato: must (unfermented or partially fermented grape juice or wine)
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mustum. Compare Romanian must, Italian mosto.

parole.significato: to adapt to, adjust to, acclimatize to
parole.testo: Mediopassive of mushtëkoj, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *domesticāre, based on domesticus (“belonging to the house”).
Learned borrowing from Latin musculus. Doublet of mushk or mushkull, which entered earlier through Vulgar Latin.
Derived from Latin medulla.

Possibly from Vulgar Latin miser (“wretch”) (see Italian misero), with the intervention of -yrë and the epenthesis of an -n- sound. Connected linguistically to Albanian mizor, which has the form minxore reflecting mynxyrë.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin muscus. Compare also Romanian mușchi, from a diminutive form.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *medicaster, from Latin medicus (“healing, medicine; doctor”), whence Albanian mjek (“doctor”), with the suffix -aster.

From Old Albanian kat (Gjon Buzuku 1499 – c. 1577), also attested as mkatë (Pjetër Budi 1566 — 1622) and mpkat (Pjetër Bogdani 1630—1689), from Latin peccātum (“sin, error, fault”). The origin of the initial nasal is unclear, yet it could either reflect the native preposition më (“in, on, at”) (earl
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mōmentum. Doublet of moment, a later borrowing.

Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin mataxa, from Ancient Greek μέταξα (métaxa). Meaning in common with Eastern Romance: compare Romanian mătase (“silk”), however different than Dalmatian matuos and Italian matassa (“skein, hank”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin manica. Compare Romanian mânecă, Spanish manga.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *manuāria, from Latin manuārius (“belonging to the hand”).
Borrowed from Latin mīror (“to be astonished at, marvel at, admire, be amazed at, wonder at”).
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin migrāre, with metathesis. Cf. also mergō, mergere and Romanian merge (“to go”).

parole.significato: (of livestock, animals) to rest at noon
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin merīdiō. Compare regional Romanian meriza, Aromanian amiridz.
From earlier mishërier, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin miseria (“wretchedness”).

First attested in Matrënga's catechism as të mbëshuarë (“load, burden”). A prefixed form of pëshoj, a variation of the standard peshoj (“to weigh”), itself verbalized from peshë (“weight”), from Latin pēnsum (“id.”). Compare mësoj and pësoj for morphological development.

parole.significato: silver birch, European white birch (Betula pendula)
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Late Latin mastichinus (“gummy”) (compare Romanian mesteacăn (“birch”), Sicilian mastigona (“piney thistle”)), from Ancient Greek μαστίχινος (mastíkhinos), from μαστίχη (mastíkhē, “mastic”).
Borrowed from Latin meditari.
Borrowed from Latin nātūra.
Disputed: * Variant of dëkoj. * Borrowed from Latin indīcāre (“to impose, to inflict”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin indulgēre (“to be indulgent, to concede”).
Borrowed from Latin mātrīcula in the sense of early Medieval Latin mātrīna.
A prefixal derivative of *dëshkoj, from Latin dēspicārī (“to despise”), from dēspiciō.
From Vulgar Latin *incarrico. Compare Aromanian ncarcu, Romanian încărca.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin unguere (“to anoint, smear with oil”).
From Latin ieiūnō (“to fast”); semantic development from 'to not eat' to 'to taste only'. See also Gheg ngjinoj. Ultimately a doublet of agjëroj.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin ingrātus.
Variant of nguloj, from ngul. Phonetically also possibly from the Vulgar Latin *incuneō, from Latin cuneō. Compare Romanian încuia.
Per Çabej from gur (“stone”) + -oj, literally "to stiffen, become petrified"; contaminated by gurrë for expressive reasons. For Orel from Latin incurrere (“to commit (a fault)”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin angustus. Compare Romanian îngust, Aromanian ngustu. Doublet of inherited angësht.
From Old Albanian *engushullonj, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin consōlō.
From ninë (“cradle”) + -ullë, from Vulgar Latin. Compare Italian ninna (“lullaby”) and Sardinian ninna (“cradle”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin noverca.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin in offulā, from offula (“small bit”); compare Neapolitan gnuòffele, guòffole (“jawbone”).
Derivative of *nokë, borrowed from Latin innocuus (“harmless, innocent”)

parole.significato: swim, swimming (act of swimming or ability to swim)
parole.testo: From a deverbal of Latin natāre, *notāre, compare Italian nuoto. A direct verbal borrowing would have regularly yielded **nëtoj instead of attested notoj, which must be a secondary derivation from the noun. Earliest attestations start with /mn/, likely due rebracketing of expressions such as i bie m
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Aromanian anot, Romanian înota. Displaced native Albanian luoz.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *anulla, from Latin anus (“old woman”).
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin numerus. Compare Romanian număr, with a similar pronunciation.
From numër, or borrowed from Latin numerō. Often replaces njeh (“id.”) in everyday speech.
Variant of nyje, singularized plural of Old Albanian nye, neu, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin nōdus.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin reiterāre (“to repeat”).
Calque of Latin November, from nëntë (“nine”) + -or.
Ultimately from Late Latin Oasis, from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”).

parole.significato: ode: lyric poem or solemn song
parole.testo: Ultimately from Late Latin oda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).
Learned borrowing from Latin offendō, from the compounding of the prefix ob- and *fendō.
Borrowed from Latin officium.
Ultimately from Latin offerō.

parole.significato: round mud firepan/vessel used for cooking
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin rotundum (“sphere, round”) (see Italian rotondo); taking a supporting vowel before the -rt- sound.
Borrowed from Latin hōra, ultimately from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra). Doublet of herë.

Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin baptizō (“to baptize”) with unclear phonological development. Topalli suggests contamination from bagëm (“anointing oil, unction”). Orel suggests a combination of dissimilation and shift of voicedness. Derived from Ancient Greek βαπτίζω (baptízō, “to dip, plu
Orel derives it from Latin pactō; cf. hoc pactō (“this way”), aliō pactō (“otherwise”).

From pajt (“thanks to”) + -oj. According to Meyer and Miklosich "pajtoj" was borrowed from (unattested) Vulgar Latin *pāctāre, which derived from Latin pāx (“peace”). Latin pāx was borrowed into Albanian as paqe (“peace”) - from which actually the alternative terms paqtoj and paqoj derived. Orel der
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pallia < pallium.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin paucus (“few, little”).
Ultimately from Latin particula.
From Latin pāla (“shovel, spade”).
From dialectal palnjë, from *paltën + -jë, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *plātinus (compare Romanian paltin (“sycamore maple”)), from Latin platanus (“plane tree”).
Borrowed from Latin pāx, pācem (“peace”).
Borrowed from Latin paradīsus.
Calque of Latin princeps, using parë.
Borrowed from Late Latin parlamentum.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin apparamentum (“preparation, preparing”), from apparare.
from Latin paradisus
Ultimately from Medieval Latin partīta (“part, party”), from Latin partīta, feminine of partītus, past participle of partīrī (“to divide”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha).
Early borrowing through Vulgar Latin from Latin pōma (“fruit, fruit tree”).
Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin poeniteō, from Latin paeniteō, with a later suffix within Albanian.
Borrowed from Latin poenitēre.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pinna. Displaced native Albanian perk.
From Latin pignus.

parole.significato: hindrance, obstacle, hurdle, impediment, barrier, encumbrance, impasse
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin pedica.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin impedicō.
Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.
Learned borrowing from Latin perinaeum.
Related to or from Latin parentō (“to sacrifice, revenge a death”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin piscis. Compare Aromanian peashti, pescu, Romanian pește, Italian pesce.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *pescopus from Latin episcopus.
From a derivative of Latin pēnsō.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pensāre. Doublet of pincar (“to think”), which was borrowed through Sicilian.
From earlier *penshë, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pensum. For the loss of /s, ʃ/ before /n/, cf. pesë < older *pensë.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pendulus, from pendere (“to hang, suspend”).
Ultimately from Latin pergula. Compare Italian pergola, Aromanian pergurã.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *pesca, from Latin persicum.

From Vulgar Latin pettia, pettium. Ultimate origin uncertain; perhaps from Transalpine Gaulish (compare Welsh peth, Breton pez (“thing”), Irish cuid (“part”)). Compare Italian pezza, French pièce, English piece, Spanish pieza, Portuguese peça.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin plāga. Compare Romanian plagă, Aromanian pleagã.
Borrowed from Latin planta (“plant”), according to Topalli (2017) who does not explain the semantic shift. Compare Venetan piantada (“plantation”) and piantareła (“row of vines”).
From Vulgar Latin *planticus, from Latin plantō (“to set, to plant”).
From Latin planca (“board, slab”).
Possibly borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin phalanga (“roller or pole for moving heavy objects”). Cf. also plang however.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *plōpus, from Latin pōpulus. Compare Italian pioppo, Romanian plop.
From Vulgar Latin plictum (“fold, pleat”); akin to Old French pleit.
From Vulgar Latin *plagium. Compare Italian piaggia, Romanian plai, and the like.
From *plëhur, from Latin pulvis.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin plumbum (“lead”).

parole.significato: people (a group of persons forming or belonging to a particular nation etc.)
parole.testo: Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin populus.
From po. Alternatively from Latin porrō (“then, moreover; but”), the loss of the final -r a result of the permanent unstressed position of the conjunction.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin porta.
A phonosemantic calque of Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), using pranë (“near, close”) + verë (“summer”), the latter derived from Vulgar Latin *vēra (“spring”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin praeda.
Probably from Latin praeda. Cf. also pre however.

parole.significato: prefect, particularly the governor of an Albanian county or (historical) prefecture.
parole.testo: Recent borrowing, ultimately from Latin praefectus (“one placed in charge”), from praeficere (“to place in charge”).

parole.significato: prefecture, especially (politics, historical) as a former first-level administrative division of Albania
parole.testo: Ultimately from Latin praefectūra (“prefecture”), from praefectus (“prefect”) + -tura (“-ure: forming nouns”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *preptо̄ for *praebitor (compare Aromanian preftu, Romanian preot), from Latin presbyter.
From Latin praeīre.
From Latin porrīna, a derivative of Latin porrum (“chives, leek”).
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin, from Latin Aprīlis. Compare popular Romanian prier (“April”), Aromanian aprir, prilj.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin parēns, parentem. Compare Romanian părinte, Italian parente.
From Vulgar Latin *prince(s), from Latin prīnceps.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin prōdāre.
Ultimately from Latin prophēta, from Ancient Greek προφήτης (prophḗtēs, “one who speaks for a god”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + φημί (phēmí, “to tell”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin parāre (“to make ready, defend”). Compare French parer, Italian parare.

Typically considered a borrowing from Vulgar Latin brocca (“fork, roasting-spit”), from Latin broccus, but with unusual devoicing of the anlaut. Compare French broche, Italian brocca. However, the devoicing may have taken place in Greek πρόκα (próka) (which see for details) by a common process of ba
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin proximāre (“to come near, approach”), with a complicated semantic development; 'to get close' > 'to know intimately' > 'to slander'. Equates to prozhëm + -oj.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin proximus, with "nearest forest" → "community forest".
From Latin publica. Cf. Serbo-Croatian puk.
A secondary variant of pëllas (derived from Latin palātium), with the hypercorrect voicing of the auslaut. According to Meyer a variant of lëpozë ~ lëpizë.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pulpa. Compare Romanian pulpă.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pollicāris, from pollex.
Borrowed from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine of Latin pullus (compare French poule).
Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin puteum. Compare Romanian puț, Italian pozzo.
Borrowed from a Vulgar Latin *posāre, from Latin pausāre (“I halt, cease, pause”).
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin potestātem, accusative singular of potestās.

Borrowed from Vulgar Latin *potestāre, from Latin potestās (“power, ability”), whence Albanian pushtet (“power”). Cognate with Medieval Latin potestare (“to control”), Old French poëster (“to exercise power, to govern, to dominate; to put in power”), Italian podestare. The dialectal forms poshtroj,
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin pavicula ("rammer").

From an earlier *pëdyll, borrowed from Late Latin padūlem (“swamp”), from a metathesis of Latin palūdem. Compare Romanian pădure, which shows the same change in meaning. Compare also Italian padule, which keeps the Latin sense. Otherwise cognate or derived from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phúllon, “leaf”)
From Latin palātium.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin palumbus. Compare Italian palombo, Aromanian pãrumbu, Romanian porumb.
Based on *gjëroj, borrowed through Vulgar Latin from Latin jūrāre.
Borrowed through Vulgar Latin *paraula from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Compare also Romanian paraulă.

parole.significato: to be too lazy to do something, go to work, etc.
